content: When capturing data as a digital image, personal identifying information can be excluded by physically covering this information before the image is taken. In retrospective data collection using multiple routine data sources, patient codes or personal identifying information may be temporarily required to exclude duplicate records or to link records from different sources to create a complete surveillance dataset. Once the data collection purpose is fulfilled, personal identifying information should be permanently deleted from the dataset. For example, the primary source of surveillance data may be the antenatal clinic (ANC) register. However, test results for individual tests in the HIV diagnostic algorithm may only be available in a laboratory or HIV testing and counseling (HTC) register. The surveillance program would need to match data from these two routine sources to create a full record for each eligible pregnant woman. To achieve this, the ANC number for each record abstracted from the ANC register could be collected. This number could then be used to locate the same women in the laboratory or HTC register and extract the results for each individual test in the HIV diagnostic algorithm. After this process, the ANC number would be removed from the surveillance data collection form. Retrospective data collection based on electronic medical record (EMR) systems leverages existing, accessible, individual-level electronic data on pregnant women attending ANC. In this approach, the surveillance team collaborates with the EMR data manager to identify and extract records of eligible pregnant women visiting surveillance sites during the surveillance period. Quality assurance during surveillance data collection is critical to ensure the reliability of surveillance estimates. Data collectors and field coordinators are responsible for conducting quality assurance as part of the surveillance data collection procedures. Surveillance data should only be collected from eligible women during the defined surveillance period, accurately and completely abstracted from routine program data tools, and managed securely as per protocol. Sampling methods and sample-size requirements for records of eligible pregnant women must also adhere to the protocol. Real-time data collection may offer advantages in certain settings. In this approach, data are collected in real time as pregnant women visit the site, similar to methods used in unlinked anonymous testing (UAT) serosurveillance, but without aliquoting biological specimens for surveillance. This method allows for increased control over surveillance inputs, such as routine program data, routine HIV testing, and routine syphilis testing. Surveillance staff can monitor and support the quality of these inputs in real time, making this method suitable for countries where the quality of routine data is inconsistent across ANC sites. However, this method requires significantly more time and resources for training and monitoring ANC site staff throughout the surveillance period. In real-time data collection, ANC staff themselves act as data collectors, routinely recording data in site data tools (e.g., registers, maternal cards) and abstracting these data for surveillance in real time as pregnant women visit ANC sites. This increases the number of data collectors involved in surveillance. ANC staff at all surveillance sites must be trained and monitored to identify eligible pregnant women, collect data according to protocol, and ensure the security of surveillance data during collection and storage until retrieval by field coordinators. Field coordinators oversee data collection by ANC staff at all surveillance sites, primarily through site visits. Consecutive sampling of eligible pregnant women is preferred for real-time data collection due to its simplicity in field implementation. Sampling begins on the first day of the surveillance period and continues until a defined sample size is reached. If all surveillance variables are not available in a single routine data tool, the data collection flow should be designed to collect variables from multiple routine data tools. For example, the ANC register may be the primary routine data source for surveillance data, but results for individual tests in the HIV diagnostic algorithm may only be available in a laboratory or HTC register. In such cases, the surveillance program must devise a data collection flow that allows the surveillance data collection form to capture information from both the ANC register and the laboratory or HTC register for each eligible pregnant woman. Regardless of the surveillance design or data collection method, HIV surveillance among pregnant women attending ANC based on routine data is likely to encounter routine records with missing data. These records should still be collected, and missing, inconsistent, or invalid values should be checked against data collection forms or digital images and corrected. All corrections must be documented. Robust data management practices are essential to ensure the integrity of surveillance data, the reliability of surveillance estimates, and the confidentiality of pregnant women whose routine data are collected for surveillance. All electronic devices, digital images, and databases should be encrypted, password-protected, and accessible only to appropriate surveillance staff. Surveillance databases should be regularly backed up on a secure external system and securely preserved for future analysis. Data entry should be performed by trained clerks under the supervision of a data manager. Electronic data entry screens should match the format of data collection tools, and all data should be entered twice (double data entry) to allow for verification of accuracy. Discrepancies should be resolved by checking paper forms or digital images. During data entry, data files should be regularly backed up. Data cleaning involves producing frequency tables for each ANC site and surveillance variable to identify data quality issues originating from data collection or entry. Missing, inconsistent, or invalid values should be checked against data collection forms or digital images and corrected, with all corrections documented. Methods for analyzing data from HIV surveillance among pregnant women attending ANC are presented, including calculating site prevalence. Site prevalence is calculated by dividing the number of HIV-positive pregnant women (including those newly tested positive or previously known to be HIV-positive) by the number of pregnant women with known HIV status. These methods can also be applied to calculate syphilis measures.
